Sue Grand   Faculty and supervisor at the NYU Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis; faculty of the Psychoanalytic Institute of Northern California, and Associate Editor of Psychoanalytic Dialogues. She is the author of The Reproduction of Evil: A Clinical and Cultural Perspective. She is in private practice in NYC and in Teaneck, NJ.
war; hero; atrocity; soldier; counter-transference

Entwining history with clinical process, this paper investigates the gendering of war, and of war resistance. Cultural rhetoric of war relies on constructing an eroticized fusion between heroic performance and civilian desire. This fusion occludes real perception of the war zone. War resistance must break up this erotic fusion, and restore absent images of combat. Gendered protests are necessary to achieve this. This process is traced through war reportage, protest activity, and a clinical study of a “war hero” who recounts an atrocity. Erotic fusion ignites in the analytic dyad, and is broken up by the appearance of an omniscient maternal specter.

Editors' Introduction to Commentaries on State Regulation of Psychoanalysis

Lynne Layton and Simon Clarke

Simon Clarke

Brookline, MA, USA.

Simon Clarke  

In our last issue, 11/3, we published Jan De Vos's strong polemic against French and Belgian psychoanalysts' reactions to state moves to regulate psychoanalysis. De Vos critiqued French analysts, including Jacques-Alain Miller, for, among other things, missing the historic opportunity to differentiate psychoanalysis from a scientistic and medicalized psychology. We also published Jacques China's review of a conference in the UK on the topic of state regulation of psychoanalysis. These papers revealed striking differences between the way analysts view the issue: differences, for example, between those who insist that psychoanalysis is not a mental health discipline at all, those who believe it is a mental health discipline but want to regulate its standards internally and keep the state out, and those who welcome state attempts to protect mental health “consumers” by creating standards of care and procedures for complaints. Given the importance of the topic in the history of psychoanalysis, and the widely disparate views, we invited three analysts to comment further on the issue. Laurel Bass Wagner and Ona Nierenberg take divergent views on recent events in New York State, where a group of psychoanalysts themselves lobbied for a state law to regulate the practice of psychoanalysis and were successful. Both Wagner and Nierenberg are critical of this move, but each formulates the stakes of the move quite differently. Ian Parker discusses the situation in the UK, focusing on the contentious issues of “evidence based practices” and complaints procedures. The issues are complex and of great importance to the future of psychoanalysis. We welcome further conversation on the topic.

Lynne Layton and Simon Clarke

Brookline, MA, USA.

Nick Tingle's Self-Development and College Writing utilizes psychoanalytic theory to present an effective analysis of the subjective issues facing college students and composition faculty in contemporary writing courses. Tingle's central thesis is that in order for students to become productive writers of academic prose, they must pass through a difficult stage of psychological development. Drawing primarily from the works of Heinz Kohut and Robert Kegan, Tingle develops a convincing psychological and cultural theory of student learning. Moreover, this work is one of the first texts in the field of composition to combine an attention to the subjectivity of composing students with a close examination of the subjectivity of writing teachers.

According to Tingle, when composition faculty ask their students to enter into academic discourse, these teachers are motivating their students to take on a new relationship with language, and this new relationship requires a developmental shift requiring a destabilizing change in identity and cognition. In other terms, learning to master academic prose does not only require learning new cognitive skills; rather, the types of writing that we often want our students to perform is dependent on the ability of students to move to a higher level of consciousness, and this developmental move is fraught with anxiety for both the students and their teachers. In short, academic writing requires students to give up their commonsense understandings of culture and language in order to grasp a more theoretical and abstract conception of reality.

Since Tingle sees the movement towards academic writing as highly destabilizing and anxiety-provoking, he turns to the field of Self-Psychology and to the notion that the classroom is a holding environment or transitional space. The key to this theory of learning and psychological development is the role played by the teacher's empathy in supporting the student through the difficult task of reaching beyond their comfortable levels of knowledge and identity-formation. Moreover, central to the teacher's empathy for Tingle is the role played by the “being” of the teacher and the teacher's ability to get students to pay attention to their own subjective states when they read, write, and learn.

A portrayal of the Michelin Man icon as a pictograph discovered during an archeological dig may be limited to a work of fiction (Levon, 1990), yet the narrative conveys a postmodern sensibility in which historical value is suspect. Some (see Oates, 2005) have suggested that such suspicion is in fact the zeitgeist, albeit disengaged, of young highly educated urban adults. A new comic book depicts the difficulty of such a zeitgeist, as urban youth who are superheroes face confusion in regard to matters ranging from their sexuality to the use of their superhero powers, and are distressed to find that both older superheroes and their parents are in no position to mentor them (Heinberg, 2005).

Central to the thesis of the current work under review, the 27th volume in the Relational Perspectives Book Series now edited by Lewis Aron and Adrienne Harris, is the argument that a loss of meaning due to uncertainty is a central experience of contemporary young urban adults. The focus of this book is the cultural changes encountered by the cohort commonly referred to as generation X - born between 1960 and 1980 - and the impact of such a culture change on the psyche.

In The Designed Self, Carlo Strenger suggests that members of generation X live in a world different from that of the Baby Boomers. He notes changes such as shrinking populations and extended singlehood status to suggest that categories that were meaningful to the parents of current young adults are less or not at all relevant in contemporary society. Pace Lacan, Strenger argues that such a condition characterizes a culture in which fatherlessness (i.e., a lack of cultural authority) is prevalent.

hate; teachers; students; Donald Winnicott; countertransference

This paper brings Donald Winnicott's views on hatred in the countertransference to bear on pedagogical relationships between teachers and students in classroom settings. Specifically, the paper explores the ways in which teachers' affective dynamics shape their identifications with students. The question of objective vs subjective hatred is raised as a problem of ethics in teaching.

Are right and wrong common universal aspects of law that come out of our inherent nature as human beings, expressed through our common biology and the heritage of our upbringing? Or alternatively, are they merely relative to the culture one happens to live in? Fred Alford's quest is whether morality is an opinion, or a law of our nature.

Alford questions whether the contemporary and extreme emphasis on individualism has eradicated shared law or morality (Macintyre, 2000). Crisis threatens if moral certainties no longer exist, and, on the basis of our wide multiculturalism, other people are entirely at liberty to hold to their own, however diverse. The only moral good, it seems, is that one should never press one's own moral beliefs on anyone else.

In his opening essay, Alford describes how Sophocles' Antigone is torn by a dilemma - to follow a universal law decreed by the gods, or to bend to the will of the local state law. Natural morality demanded she bury her dead brother, a universal obligation above all personal opinion, but the decree by her brother's enemy, King Creon, proclaimed that she be put to death if she perform the rituals. Antigone appealed to a higher law than that of the state. Aristotle argued that she represents a pure form of natural law endowed by the Gods, fated to die in her confrontation with Creon - the universal against the local and temporal. Most mortals are confused by such conflicting demands, but, in contrast, Antigone defends natural law, and does so precisely because it brings her close to her own death - this is Alford's central argument: moral loyalty is close to the deathly forces. Natural law is only won by passing through the valley of death: “Dark eros”, Alford names it. Natural law is a far more subtly derived than the prosaic Manichean sense of an eternal war between dark and light. Although Antigone's predicament has been discussed by philosophers from Aristotle via Aquinas and Augustine to George Steiner and Alasdair Macintyre in the modern age, Alford turns to psychoanalysis, which trades in “guilt” and the “super-ego”.

The introduction to Analysts in the Trenches presents a veritable manifesto for “community psychoanalysis,” (p xiii) which the editors view as a “discrete field” within psychoanalysis (Twemlow and Parens, 2006, p 430). The editors, each a psychoanalyst engaged in community praxis, have collected a dozen chapters representing various applications of psychoanalysis to problems faced by individuals, families, and groups outside the consulting room. The biopsychosocial problems addressed in this fine collection vary from childhood violence prevention to inter-ethnic conflict to post-traumatic reactions in emergency response workers at Ground Zero.

What unites and distinguishes the various community psychoanalysis applications described in Trenches is the intention and commitment to “applying our knowledge of the influences of unconscious [my italics] processes… to population groups” (Twemlow and Parens, 2006, p 435). The authors marry theoretical and phenomenological approaches in assessing the impact of internal and external influences on development. Some might be inclined to term this work “applied psychoanalysis,” though I believe this term suggests a lesser clinical impact, more akin to applications of psychoanalysis to art and literary criticism. The editors, too, veer away from this term and consider the work they and the other authors depict as “community psychoanalysis,” a sub-field of its own whose practitioners employ “creative strategies… when assisting communities to overcome violence and the transmission of trauma” (p xiii).

This may seem a radical departure from the role of the stereotyped classical analyst sequestered in his/her consulting room, steeped in a dyadic analyst-analysand engagement. This new work serves as a “sociology of thought” that synthesizes Freud's psychoanalytic movement with the concomitant phenomenological thrust in 20th-century European thought. Askay and Farquhar attempt to trace the mergers and severances of psychoanalysis and existential phenomenology through a study of Freud's relation to Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, and Merleau-Ponty. This interesting study is bracketed by an analysis of Freudian metapsychology as grounded in Schopenhauerian metaphysics, giving the reader the possibility of understanding Freud as a Neo-Kantian (pp 194-196) and/or as developer of Schopenhauer's budding theory of the unconscious in human life (pp 103-124). Askay and Farquhar attempt to re-construct Freudian theory through its philosophical origins, and utilize this reconstructed picture of Freud to appreciate the existential critique of Freud's metapsychology. As a work in the history of thought, the authors succeed admirably. The book, however, provides few insights into the substantial debates concerning Freud's primary affections: the unconscious, the division of self, and the socio-political application of psychic phenomena.

There are three central bindings of Askay and Farquhar's work: first, a critique of Freud's metapsychology as “science” (including an explicit critique of his ambivalence toward philosophy); the correspondence of psychoanalytic theory and existential phenomenology as critiques of “the equation of consciousness with mental life” (p 90) in the history of western philosophy; and, finally, a contribution to the awareness of the hesitation in adapting Freud to existential concerns, particularly through Heidegger, Sartre, and Merleau-Ponty.

In the first instance, Askay and Farquhar repeatedly remind the reader of Freud's statement regarding the place of psychoanalysis in the philosophy/science divide: “(psychoanalysis) is part of science and can adhere to the scientific Weltanschauung” (p 21). With this statement and others, Askay and Farquhar construct a quasi-Freudian critique of Freud's (forgotten) reliance on philosophy, particularly Schopenhauerian metaphysics, in favor of his irrational clamoring to the scientific ideal. Askay and Farquhar succinctly deconstruct the Freudian “world-picture” through a series of contradictions concerning Freud's true influences. The authors list these contradictions, which include Freud's alleged distaste for philosophy's search after comprehensiveness (compared with his picture of mental life, which also aimed at completeness), Freud's “observable” science of the unobservable, and Freud's anti-systematic ideology, which conflicted with his metapsychological system (p 25). These contradictions (and others mentioned throughout the text) form the basis of Askay and Farquhar's critique of Freud's scientific posturing.

Out of the throng of voices crowding current debates on the politics of gay marriage, gay parenting, abortion and child pornography, Edelman's arises with singular force. No Future makes no explicit claim to be an “intervention” in current debates, though. Instead Edelman goes directly to the most unquestioned value of our culture - that of “the Child” in whose name queer people have been vilified and denied rights across a range of cultural and historical contexts. The Child, Edelman explains, figures an endlessly redemptive promise; redemption, that is, for a political present that can never attain fullness of meaning without this figure of the Child standing in for the promise of future plenitude. In this politically coercive dynamic, which Edelman names “reproductive futurism”, the Child represents the promise of future plenitude while excluding those who are thought to reject this imagined “future.” In overturning this last sacred cow Edelman also puts forward a radical, and psychoanalytically inspired definition of the political. Placing the political subject onto the Lacanian couch, he reminds us that the sexual and the political cannot and should not be thought separately.

No Future draws heavily on Lacanian theory, along with post-structuralist literary theory and cultural studies, to critique the reproductive futurism at the heart of all cultural discourse concerned with the political. For this reason, Edelman's critique looks to a wide range of cultural products: billboards, musicals, high literature, popular literature, Hitchcock films, and critical theory (namely the work of Judith Butler and Jean Baudrillard). Some of his more developed cultural analyses focus on popular culture figures such as Little Orphan Annie, Peter Pan and Harry Potter, while also touching on high culture figures such as Antigone and Silas Marner, which makes for an often entertaining read. His most compelling readings are of two Hitchcock films, North by Northwest and The Birds. (His interpretation of the birds in The Birds as a figure for the death drive is already canonical.)

A new metaphor and concept is proposed to comprehend massive organizational change where the inability to mourn prevails: “inconsolable organization.” The group psychodynamics of this process are explored, in part with the aid of the work of Yiannis Gabriel on the concept of “organizational miasma.” Three vignettes are used to “flesh out” the idea of an inconsolable organization. A tentative model is proposed, one that situates organizational inconsolability relative to other dimensions of adaptation to traumatic change. Recommendations are offered for assisting organizations in these circumstances.

Margaret Whilde  

In An Archive of Feelings, literary scholar Ann Cvetkovich takes on the ambitious task of reworking current and historical conceptualizations of trauma from the vantage point of lesbian countercultural formations. Drawing on a vast array of primary texts, including oral histories of lesbian AIDS activists, writings on butch-femme sexuality, and feminist performance pieces on immigration, and placing these alongside personal reflections, Freudian psychoanalytic theory, feminist self-help literature, contemporary psychiatric texts, and poststructuralist queer, feminist and critical race theory, Cvetkovich gives pride of place to a body of lesbian experiences that has traditionally been neglected within trauma studies. Cvetkovich's aspiration in the book is not so much to lend legitimacy to lesbian trauma or to advocate for its admittance into the canon of trauma studies, but rather - and more provocatively - to demonstrate how a consideration of contemporary lesbian art and activism might “give rise to different ways of thinking about trauma” (p 3).

An Archive of Feelings represents a crucial feminist and queer intervention into the field of trauma studies, a field that has, over the past decade, become increasingly dominated by a focus on massive world historical events. This emphasis on the exceptional, the colossal, and the global has obscured the powerful roles of the quotidian and the domestic in structuring psychic experience and public life. Cvetkovich's text seeks to redress this problem by enlarging the focus of trauma studies to include a broader variety of experience and by calling for a more persistent and sustained critique of “what counts as a trauma history and whose feelings matter in the national sphere” (p 37). In addition, the book invokes lesbian subcultural practices in order to mount a challenge to the tendency within contemporary scholarship and activism to pit therapeutic and political activist responses to trauma against one another, and thus contribute to the bifurcation in the cultural imagination of public and private modes of experience. It is the persistence of the division between public and private, or between emotional and political life, according to Cvetkovich, that has allowed certain kinds of trauma, such as sexual trauma or homophobia, to be consigned to the domestic sphere or the consulting room and thus to slip out of public view.

Christine Kieffer  

In this monograph, Patrick Colm Hogan, a professor in the Department of English at the University of Connecticut, examines the psychological and cultural determinants of social consent and conformity, with particular attention paid to economic inequities in contemporary America. One theme that Hogan emphasizes throughout his book is the underlying pervasiveness of subtle psychological coercion in America, while frequent lip-service is nevertheless paid to the importance of participatory democracy by its politicians.

Early in his book, Hogan takes up the important question of why more people, particularly those who (and they are in the majority) suffer economic and class inequities, do not rebel. As he attempts to demonstrate, using theory and data derived from social and cognitive psychology - and to a lesser extent, psychoanalysis - those who suffer the most from political, social and economic inequity often participate in the establishment and maintenance of their own suffering and humiliation, through the often unconscious absorption of largely unarticulated group norms.

In the first chapter, the author challenges the theory, often put forth by conservative groups, of “rational conformity” - that is, the idea that people will be motivated to do what benefits them. As Hogan repeatedly demonstrates, the masses, often in response to media manipulation, will acquiesce to policies that are clearly against their best interests, through a subtle process of identification with a ruling or leader class, and sometimes with an acceptance of a rather blatant distortion of facts. However, the author maintains that readers and viewers often will ignore their best interests as a result of an ongoing and subtle immersion in an ideological environment that “sets the terms of the debate so as to exclude certain sets of possible beliefs from consideration or discussion” (p 59). That is, the terms of debate limit the framework of what views are even considered imaginable. And once the terms of the debate are set, they tend to be self-perpetuating.

Aside from the simple curiosity of watching Lacan in action, my primary interest in this documentary video was to evaluate its pedagogical value. Would it inspire my undergraduate students to read Lacan? Would it illuminate key aspects of the psychoanalytic theory that we had been reading? Would it spark their interest or bore them? Is it a better introduction to Lacan than the previously released film, Jacques Lacan: Psychoanalysis Revisited (Kaprist and Roudinesco, 2001)? And if the answer to these questions was no, would it contribute anything to the knowledge of Lacanian scholars or clinicians, and if so what?

Jacques Lacan Speaks is comprised of two almost equal parts: the first is an edited version of a lecture Lacan delivered at the University of Louvain in 1971, and the second is edited footage of an interview he granted to the film's director, Françoise Wolff, following the lecture. The lecture was filmed during the period that Dany Nobus and Malcolm Quinn characterize as “massive intellectual performance with little or no audience participation” (2005, p 94). Arriving with crooked cigar in hand, and announcing that he has not prepared a formal lecture, Lacan proceeds to discuss some of the well-known themes: the concept of discourse, knowledge and the unconscious, and transference as love. His slightly longer discussion of death as a matter of faith is one of the highlights here, where Lacan asserts that life would be insupportable if we could not rely on the certainty of death. The problem with the lecture material is that we only get little bits of his thinking on any one theme, and many of the most interesting bits are included in the earlier film for better effect. The lecture does serve to demonstrate some of the peculiarities of Lacan's style, which Wolff later describes as “slow motion punctuated by sighs, tortuous passion, oratory, anecdotes, slang, mockery, insults, intermittent thunder, endless quibbling, massive boredom, witticisms, puns and jokes on the sublime”. More interesting is Lacan's response to the would-be revolutionary student who interrupts his talk, pours water on the desk, and makes a barely coherent speech lamenting the status quo. Lacan graciously engages him, and after the student is escorted out of the room, he continues to use the outburst as an example of how the discourse of mastery finds its way even into allegedly revolutionary positions.

A patient comes to the office for a first session, takes a deep breath, and wonders, “How to begin?” There is so much that is relevant, interrelated, and it is difficult to know where to start. Such is the feeling Linda Hopkins must have had when beginning her recently published biography of Masud Khan, False Self: The Life of Masud Khan. There are so many strands to Khan's life, from his childhood and family life in colonial India, his journey to Britain at age 22 to seek a personal analysis, his analysis with Winnicott and his editing of Winnicott's writings, his marriage to a Russian ballerina, and later the mental illness and alcoholism that tarnished his reputation and led to his isolation and death.

Like a good analyst, Hopkins listens well, and provides a wonderful holding environment for this bristling and vibrant life-story. The 400-plus pages are undoubtedly edited down - evidenced in part by nearly 100 additional pages of endnotes - and yet the book is very readable, moves quickly, and is fascinating. Given Khan's emphasis in his own clinical work on the holding environment, it is a tribute to him that Hopkins is able to contain and present Khan's rich, multi-faceted story.

Although there is one other scholarly biography of Masud Khan (Masud Khan: The Myth and the Reality, by Roger Willoughby in 2005), Hopkins was the first biographer to be granted access to a complete copy of Khan's unpublished Work Books, which are quoted extensively. Hopkins also conducted interviews with Khan's colleagues, friends, relatives, and analysands. Five chapters of the book detail Khan's clinical work from the late 1940s until 1980, drawing from interviews with analysands and supervisees who recall Khan's clinical work with them. This window into Khan's development as an analyst alone makes the book worthwhile for those interested in the history of British psychoanalysis and the technical implementation of Winnicott's and Khan's formulations of the holding environment and regression. Particularly of note is the firsthand detailing of Khan's eventual sexual boundary transgressions with patients, allowing a rare look at how a personal life in disarray and growing psychological distress led a psychoanalyst to become inappropriately involved with the patients he was treating.

Simon Clarke has written a fine primer on the intertwined themes of social theory, psychoanalysis and racism. The central thesis is that psychoanalysis deepens our understanding of sociology, and, more specifically, that getting beyond structural racism requires attention to affective forces that are best conceptualized in psychoanalysis. Clarke is not breaking new ground here; he presents ideas that most readers of this journal will find familiar and congenial. The main aim of this book is to provide an introductory guide for students: each chapter contains boxed examples/elaborations of theoretical points and a summary of key terms, and there is a background section at the end of the book, which lists suggested readings, websites, and journals. Still, Clarke's discussions of various thinkers such as Bauman, Fanon, Fromm, and especially representatives from the Kleinian tradition, are illuminating and well worth reading.

Clarke begins with a presentation of recent debates about terms such as race, racism, ethnicity, and diaspora. He contrasts those views that see racism as having its source in containing fear of the Other to those which maintain that racism is defined by exclusionary practices. He also explores modernity as the distinctive background for understanding what racism is, citing Zygmunt Bauman's notion of the “gardening state,” wherein the state uses rational design to cultivate citizens as useful plants and weed out others, brutally if necessary (p 45). Next, Clarke moves in the direction of dealing with subtle, unacknowledged aspects of racism - manifest in the example of inequities in education for Blacks in Britain. The “new racism” refrains from a discourse in which minorities are deemed inferior, in favor of an insistence on and imposition of difference.

In turning to explicate the term ethnicity, Clarke raises several concerns. While he appreciates how the term is invoked to capture a sense of common, shared culture, and even solidarity, he worries that it preserves the distinction between inclusion and exclusion in an unhelpful way. According to Clarke, those who embrace an identity in terms of ethnicity are marking their difference from the norm. The invocation of a norm that is, apparently by definition, without ethnicity is troubling, and I found myself uncomfortable with the complacency implied here. For groups that have been historically and systematically excluded, contesting the norm can be empowering and healthy. It is arguably even healthy for the norm to be challenged this way. Clarke might have given greater attention to the theme of agency: how a resilient identity can be affirmed in the face of historical and ongoing racism.

The discussion presents the idea that the contents of the social unconscious are not psychical but social in nature, and that the social unconscious stands not in opposition to a generalized individual consciousness but to social consciousness. This paper examines the psychic topography of identities of belonging for their sustainability in a plural world. By drawing on Freud's Moses and Monotheism, I will think about how collective identities are symbolic reconstructions of traumatic pasts and therefore foreclose their hybrid or cosmopolitan origins. While such insight demands a politic of generosity that considers the psychic “necessities” of stable racial identities, it also demands that we be aware of how the psychic mechanisms of survival, and the narratives and the ontologies they produce, might no longer serve their communities, or the communities with which they come into contact, well. Dissatisfied with Edward Said's postmodern/postcolonial response to the Israeli/Palestinian conflict in Freud and the Non-European, this paper offers a viewpoint that imagines political responses from the affective site of human loss and injury.

This paper uses psychoanalytic theory to understand the motivation of pro-space activists - people campaigning to increase human activity in outer space. It suggests that activists are motivated by fantasies of a spacefaring civilization, which manifest unconscious phantasies of omnipotence and fusion related to the experience of self in primary narcissism. The argument of the paper is that in order to understand this pursuit of a phantasized self, we must locate activists within the cultural conditions that encourage secondary narcissism. This is one example of how psychoanalytically informed social theory can account for the relationship between social structure and the motivation of political activists.

The article explores the idealization of rural landscape and rural life in contemporary English popular culture, raising issues that are underemphasized in earlier accounts of the rural as a stabilizing element in the social and economic order. Rural imagery has an emotional resonance in the unconscious realm of phantasy: it offers secure access to and possession of a good object. In media accounts, the countryside provides a sequestered, sensuous place of healing, although recent countryside imagery is also concrete in emotional quality, with a disturbing intensity, suggestive of Kleinian accounts of paranoid splitting. The article points to social theories of late modernity, in which the pressures and disruptions of the current socio-economic order contribute to a generalized fragmentation of consciousness. The persecutory tone of some popular accounts of the countryside is one of the consequences of this, transforming the rural world into a damaged maternal body.

Neil Altman  

A welcome development in contemporary psychoanalysis has been inter-disciplinary engagement. There has been such engagement from the beginning of the field, Freud himself drawing on the humanities and the sciences in the development of his thought and practice. Recently, there has been increased reflectiveness within psychoanalysis about the philosophical underpinnings of psychoanalytic theory and practice as the influence of hermeneutic philosophy, post-structuralism, and deconstructionism have been felt within the field. This self-critical tendency has joined up with efforts on the part of analysts and non-analysts to make explicit and rethink psychoanalytic presumptions about gender, sexual orientation, social class, and race that may reflect and reinforce oppressive social prejudices. This movement has led analysts, who previously might have unreflectively privileged the intrapsychic level of analysis, to note that the understanding of the psychological world is often skewed when account is not taken of larger social realities. It has become clear that psychoanalysis needs sociology, philosophy, and many other disciplines in order to counter these skews. But inter-disciplinary conversations raise the question of how to integrate different levels of analysis without reductionism. Are sexism, racism, and homophobia psychological phenomena that play out on a social stage? Or are they socio-economic-politically organized phenomena that infiltrate the individual psyche? Is there some way to take account of the psychic and social level in a way that respects the integrity of each level of analysis without making one level primary, the other secondary?

Farhad Dalal's book is a clearly argued and very valuable effort to bring the social level of analysis of racism into focus for a psychoanalytic audience. Dalal believes that the various psychoanalytic analyses of racism are all incomplete. For example, a psychoanalytic explanation of racism might say that white people use black people to deposit their unwanted psychic content, or that black people become the object of white people's sadistic id impulses or disapproving superego attitudes, or that difference per se arouses hatred. The crucial question that Dalal raises is: how does the category “black people” get generated in order to serve its function as an object of envy or sadism, or as a location into which to evacuate unwanted psychic content, or as a focus of superego condemnation? For this, Dalal says, we need to consider social and historical forces. Perhaps the central point that Dalal wants the reader to take away from his book is that racism consists essentially in an uncritical acceptance and adoption of racial categories. From this point of view, perhaps all or most of the psychoanalytic literature on race is, in fact, racist, to the extent that there is a failure to interrogate the processes by which racist categories get generated.

I take racism to be a typical example of a social phenomenon of intolerance and prejudice. It is also a state of the mind of an individual. This paper will explore the relation between intolerant attitudes such as racism on one hand, and, on the other, states of mind that are felt to be intolerable. As racist attitudes impact on the individual, what exactly in the individual do they impact upon? And how in turn do they recreate social groups characterized by that species of intolerance? I shall present clinical material to demonstrate the existence of a connection between these two phenomena, intolerance and the intolerable. Two forms of this identification - a rigid permanent form and a more flexible form - are identified from two psychoanalytic cases briefly described.

The goal of this paper is to provide an argument in defense of slave reparations from a Kleinian psychoanalytic perspective. Drawing on the work of Frantz Fanon and Melanie Klein, this paper identifies a primary aggressive guilt structure at the heart of American anti-black racism. Having identified this structure it then proceeds to argue that there is good reason to believe that the payment of reparations will allow for the engagement of white guilt such that its aggressive manifestation may be alleviated. Through this process a position shift in the attitude of white America to black America will allow for meaningful mourning and healing.

In this article, the author questions psychoanalytic responses to interracial relationships and subjectivity. She argues that much psychoanalytic discussion on interraciality has been shaped by denial and repression of race, fears of miscegenation, and normative assumptions about the superiority of endogamy. From the perspective of hybridity studies and analytic frameworks predicated on the primacy of relationality, it is time to ask different psychoanalytic questions.

Robert Chernomas

Robert Chernomas

508 Fletcher Argue Building, Winnipeg, Canada R3T 5V5
E-mail: chernoma@cc.umanitoba.ca

Robert Chernomas   Professor of economics at the University of Manitoba. He has published in both the academic and popular literature with respect to macroeconomics, the history of economic thought, health care economics, and the socio-economic determinants of health.
nurses; psychotic anxieties; taylorist alienation

The Isabel Menzies Lyth hypothesis posits that the organization of the hospital is constructed so as to defend nurses from their psychotic anxieties. Institutional arrangements allow a “rational madness” which is beyond reform, because reform might lead to a deconstruction of the institutions. I argue, alternatively, that the institution has been organized in the interests of its owners and/or managers, the result of which is to exacerbate nurses’ anxieties. Corporate/Taylorist approaches exacerbate fragmentation and encourage primitive defenses. A non-corporate/Taylorist organization would be conducive to less regressive psychological functioning and would stir up less anxiety, albeit at the expense of corporate-managerial control.

The replacement of the crime of lynching with juridical models of criminality has enabled forgetting of its collectivity. Popular discourse about lynching seems to remember it as a hate crime in anti-racist narratives or legal execution in racist narratives. Neither substitution captures the collectivity of the crimes. The juridical language of these substitutions cannot explain the collective appeal for the bloodthirsty crowds of lynchings. Using lynching photography from James Allen's Without Sanctuary: Lynching Photography in America, my paper reconstructs the collective nature of lynching as a site for psychoanalytic and cultural analysis. This article examines the concept of the analytic third in psychoanalysis and psychoanalytically informed organizational change. The analytic third is often defined as the psychological (triangular) space between self and other, subject and object, fantasy and reality - the third dimension that emerges from two persons fully engaged in the exploration of unconscious meanings, reasons, motives and actions. In neo-Kleinian object relations, it is viewed as the intersubjective dimension of transference and counter-transference, or the emergence in analytic work of the observation and experience of “I-as-subject” and “Me-as-object” (Ogden, 1994). The analytic third is what we create when we make genuine contact with one another at a deeper emotional level of experience whether in dyads, groups, communities, or organizations. It might be understood as akin to but not synonymous with Winnicott's (1971) notion of the transitional and potential space, where culture, play, creativity and imagination, reside. A case illustration is provided to better articulate the nature of the analytic third in the processes of observing, participating, and intervening in organizations.

Anal sex between men has been constructed in many ways throughout the last century. In this paper, I describe three realms of discourse that have offered ideas regarding the meanings and motivations of anal sex: (1) Freud's exploration of anal erotism using classical psychoanalytic language, (2) a radical sex theorist describing transcendence and community through anal sexuality, and (3) a Lacanian perspective that questions the idea of the anus as passive. Freud's construct of the Oedipus complex has become deeply embedded into clinical and western cultural discourses, but in a truncated form that excludes the negative Oedipal constellation. Contrary to the assumption that Freud's interest in the child's same-sex passions was of theoretical value only, a look at his case studies, and at memoirs of those analysed by Freud, suggests otherwise. All over the world, new state laws are emerging to regulate the practice of psychoanalysis and the education of psychoanalysts. While, without question, this development is overdetermined, we can recognize it as a symptom of the psychoanalytic movement with its own problematic institutions and regulations. Because there is a new law in New York state which was initiated by a group of psychoanalysts as a response to the US history of restrictive institutionalized psychoanalysis, we have an invaluable opportunity to consider state regulation from the perspective of the internal resistances to psychoanalysis. In this paper, I use the case of the New York Law to illuminate how the misunderstanding of the question of lay analysis has provoked legislation creating a new mental health profession in the place of the “impossible profession,” threatening the continued obfuscation of the specificity of psychoanalysis as Freud conceived it.
